newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FORECAST - Malaysia ringgit seen pulling out of slump.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Malaysia ringgit seen pulling out of slump.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit is expected to put a recent selloff against the dollar behind it and resume its climb, economists said on Thursday.
They said the ringgit remained inherently strong, having retained most of its gains against currencies like the yen and the Singapore dollar.
It has gained 3.55 percent against the Singapore dollar this year and 9.2 percent against the yen, riding a wave of international confidence in the Malaysian economy.

But recent central bank curbs on lending for property and share buying, a rise in U.S. interest rates and consequent bullishness in dollar/yen trade triggered a ringgit selloff this week that has wiped out much of its gains against the dollar.
"None of the factors (which affected the ringgit) is long-term," said Andrew Fung, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore.

"The selloff in the ringgit was partly overreaction to the various concerns in the market. It was initiated by large funds unwinding their positions and supported by the rise in dollar/yen and a rebound in the Singapore dollar."
After rising 2.2 percent to 2.4680 to the U.S. dollar this year, the ringgit fell to a low of 2.5120 on Wednesday. It was at 2.5250 on December 31, 1996.
Intervention by the central Bank Negara on Wednesday helped the ringgit to recover. It was at 2.5055/65 at 0630 GMT on Thursday.
Fung said the timing of the ringgit's rise would depend on when the focus shifted away from dollar/yen trade.

"While the technical picture and continued interest from U.S. funds to dump ringgit may suggest that...(an) uptrend may be delayed, the medium-term scenario still (favours ringgit)," research firm I.D.E.A said in a report.
It said that by intervening on Wednesday, the central bank has reaffirmed its preference for a strong ringgit. This was also supported by the country's trade deficit profile.
Japan accounted for nearly 28 percent of Malaysia's imports, and only 12 percent of its exports. This widened Malaysia's trade gap with Japan to 29.5 billion ringgit in 1995.
The ringgit's 12.75 percent appreciation against the yen last year has reduced the two countries' trade gap considerably, I.D.E.A said.
Being highly import dependent, Malaysian export competitiveness did not improve with the ringgit's fall, the reserch firm said.

"Contrary to what one might think, the depreciation in the ringgit does not lead to higher exports because they are highly import intensive," said Dilip Ratha, regional economist with W.I. Carr in Singapore.

"Under this scenario then, plus Bank Negara's ongoing desire to pare rates of credit growth, it would hardly be a surprise to see the central bank guiding domestic interbank rates higher through much of the year," I.D.E.A said.
"This shift in expectations should encourage greater ringgit exposure and set the domestic currency on track for a return to 2.45 (to the dollar) levels, possibly in a quite explosive fashion."
